Refraining gives zero. Return {"index":i,"profit":[num_string,den_string]} for the highest expected net profit PER OPPORTUNITY. Choose index −1 for zero/no positive profit (including empty quotes); among strictly positive tied quotes choose the LOWEST original index. Profit is an exact reduced rational with positive denominator, canonical decimal strings and zero=["0","1"]. Preserve all lists; use O(m) arithmetic operations and O(1) auxiliary integer state for m rows. Do not simulate, sort, round or optimise only per-fill edge.
explanation: Use the joint state-and-order branch probabilities specific to EACH quote. Its profit numerator is w_low l_low(ask−fee−low)+w_high l_high(ask−fee−high), over the common positive WD. Compare numerators directly; begin with the zero no-quote alternative and replace only on a strictly greater value. This preserves earliest positive ties and prefers refraining at zero. A rare favourable fill can lose to a more frequent modest edge when compared per opportunity. A quote with no reachable fills has zero profit, with no need to divide by its fill mass. One scan is O(m) arithmetic/O(1) auxiliary integer state; it does not derive demand curves from price or assert real-world optimality.

title: Learn from orders while respecting inventory limits
prompt:
low<high are integer terminal payments in [−10^9,10^9]. ONE hidden V is fixed for the whole game. weights=[w_low,w_high] are nonnegative integers ≤10^9, positive total W, describing its prior. quotes contains at most three [bid,ask,rows] entries, with −10^9≤bid≤ask≤10^9 and rows=[[customer_buy,customer_sell,no_order] in low, same in high]. All counts are integers in [0,100]. Every row of EVERY quote sums to the SAME integer D in [1,100], so its entry divided by D is the event probability conditional on V and that quote. Customers’ events are conditionally independent given V and selected quotes; menus/counts stay fixed.

At each of 0≤horizon≤5 opportunities choose one whole quote or SKIP. Skip gives no cash, inventory change or observation, and uses that opportunity. After quoting you observe buy, sell OR no order. Customer buy: dealer cash ask−fee, q changes by −1. Customer sell: dealer cash −bid−fee, q changes by +1. No order: cash zero, q unchanged, but Bayes still updates. Initial inventory is integer q in [−limit,limit], 0≤limit≤5. Exclude a quote if ANY positive-probability event under CURRENT beliefs would breach the limit; no retroactive rejection of an executed branch. fee and penalty are integers in [0,10^9]. Financing is zero. Final objective is accumulated cash plus qV MINUS penalty×q², in one currency unit. There is no interim penalty or wealth/capital constraint.

Return {"gain":[numerator_string,denominator_string],"action":index}. Gain is the EXACT best expected final objective minus the expectation from skipping EVERY opportunity with the original inventory. Reduce to canonical decimal strings, positive denominator, zero=["0","1"]. action is the optimal FIRST quote index, or −1 for skip; ties prefer skip, then the lowest quote index. At horizon zero return zero gain/action −1. Choose subsequent actions using only observed history, not V. Preserve every input. Use a finite-horizon belief/inventory recursion; memoisation may identify scaled equivalent beliefs. A conservative tree bound is \(O(m(1+3m)^h)\) arithmetic operations and \(O((1+3m)^h)\) memo states for m quotes/h opportunities (handle m=0 separately). These explicit small limits support exact computation; no polynomial/unbounded-horizon claim. Do not use float posteriors, a greedy immediate edge or simulation.
explanation:
Write \(v_0=\mathrm{low}\), \(v_1=\mathrm{high}\) and \(\lambda=\mathrm{penalty}\). For each quote, \(L_{0e}\) and \(L_{1e}\) are its low/high ROW COUNTS for event e, with common row total D; the event probabilities are these counts divided by D. Conditional beliefs can be stored as two nonnegative integer weights \(u=(a,b)\), with positive sum \(U=a+b\). At t remaining opportunities define an INTEGER value numerator \(N_t\) so expected future cash plus terminal marked inventory/penalty is \(N_t/(UD^t)\). The terminal numerator is

\[N_0(u,q)=q(av_0+bv_1)-\lambda q^2 U.\]

Skip has candidate D times the t−1 numerator. For a quoted event e, let \(c_e\) be dealer cash received and \(\delta_e\) the inventory increment; set \(u_e=(aL_{0e},bL_{1e})\) and \(z_e=aL_{0e}+bL_{1e}\). Its contribution to the common numerator is

\[c_e z_e D^{t-1}+N_{t-1}(u_e,q+\delta_e).\]

Sum the reachable event contributions and maximise over feasible quotes and skip. This cancels posterior normalising denominators exactly. A zero-mass event supplies no constraint or continuation; a reachable limit breach invalidates the entire quote. No-order branches have zero cash but can move the posterior and change future choices. Scaling \(u\) by \(g\) scales \(N_t\) by \(g\) without changing its chosen action, so cache gcd-normalised beliefs and multiply the cached numerator back by g when using it in the parent. Omitting that factor corrupts branch weights. Compare exact integer candidates, replacing only on a strict improvement to preserve skip/earliest ties. At the root subtract the original hold-to-settlement objective, including its original penalty, using the same denominator. Past cash need not be cached because it is additive and does not change feasible future actions here. Sample one gives gain five after A, versus four after greedy B; no order is precisely the observation identifying the zero state. The exponential tree bound, memo storage and integer bit costs are separate from the small declared horizon; this is not a realistic fitted market or a universal market-making policy.

title: Keep an observed payment or pay for a fresh one
prompt: You may KEEP observed, an integer in [−10^9,10^9], or pay integer cost in [0,10^9] to take a compulsory independent fresh payment. payoffs and weights are equally long integer lists of length 1..100000: payoffs in [−10^9,10^9], weights in [0,10^9] with positive sum W; fresh state i has probability weights[i]/W. observed need not belong to this fresh support. There are no other options, costs, capital constraints or financing charges; no fee is paid when keeping. Maximise conditional expected remaining payment MINUS any fee incurred now. Return {"action":"keep" or "reroll","value":[numerator_string,denominator_string]}. Keep on an EXACT tie. Value must be an exact reduced rational with positive denominator and canonical decimal strings; zero=["0","1"], integer values use denominator "1". Preserve both lists. Use \(O(n)\) arithmetic operations/O(1) auxiliary integers; do not simulate or use floats. Past sunk fees are outside this remaining-payment objective.
explanation: The compulsory fresh mean is its weighted sum divided by W, and the fee is incurred only on continuation. Compare observed×W with the continuation numerator N−cost×W. A greater-or-equal kept value implements the exact tie rule; no subtraction from the kept branch is warranted. Reduce only the chosen continuation fraction. Decimal strings preserve large exact values in the browser. One weighted pass is \(O(n)\) arithmetic/O(1) auxiliary integer state; multiplication/gcd have magnitude-dependent bit costs. A large possible fresh outcome is not its expected value.

title: Backward induction with an ordered fee schedule
prompt: Before a compulsory first draw, maximise expected final numerical payment minus optional reroll fees. payoffs and weights describe a FIXED finite law used by every independent fresh draw: equally long integer lists, length 1..1000, payoffs in [−10^9,10^9], weights in [0,10^9] with positive total W. Duplicated payoff values and zero weights are permitted. costs is an ordered list of at most 30 nonnegative integers ≤10^9. After the first observation you may keep it or pay costs[0] to discard it and draw again. After that observation you may keep or pay costs[1], and so on; a draw after the last paid reroll is compulsory with no remaining options. A fee is paid ONLY when that option is taken. No financing, wealth constraints or other costs. Keep at ties. Return {"value":[num_string,den_string],"threshold":[num_string,den_string] or None}. value is optimal expected NET payment BEFORE the first observation; threshold is the first-observation continuation value, so reroll exactly when observed<threshold. With no options threshold=None and value is the compulsory mean. All defined rationals must be exact reduced canonical decimal strings with positive denominator, zero=["0","1"]. Preserve all lists. Use O(n(k+1)) arithmetic operations/O(1) working integers for k fees, apart from input/output; integer bit costs grow with horizon. Iterate backward, not through all draw histories, and do not charge every listed fee on every path.
solution:
from math import gcd

def rational(numerator, denominator):
    divisor = gcd(abs(numerator), denominator)
    return [str(numerator // divisor), str(denominator // divisor)]

def solve(payoffs, weights, costs):
    mass = sum(weights)
    numerator = sum(v*w for v,w in zip(payoffs,weights))
    denominator = mass
    factor = gcd(abs(numerator),denominator)
    numerator //= factor
    denominator //= factor
    threshold = None
    for cost in reversed(costs):
        future = numerator - cost*denominator
        threshold = rational(future,denominator)
        numerator = sum(w*max(v*denominator,future) for v,w in zip(payoffs,weights))
        denominator *= mass
        factor = gcd(abs(numerator),denominator)
        numerator //= factor
        denominator //= factor
    return {'value': [str(numerator),str(denominator)], 'threshold': threshold}
explanation: Begin with the compulsory last draw mean. For the next fee c encountered BACKWARD, suppose the later fresh draw WITH all of its remaining choices has value N/d. Current continuation is (N−cd)/d. The current fresh value is the weighted mean of max(v_i,continuation), not max(mean,continuation). Form its numerator as \(\sum_iw_i\max\{v_i d,N-cd\}\) and denominator Wd, then reduce. The last backward iteration corresponds to costs[0], and its saved continuation is the first threshold. With no costs the initial mean survives and threshold is undefined. Sunk prior fees are additive constants under this cash objective. One pass per decision layer uses O(n(k+1)) arithmetic and O(1) working integers; exact denominators can grow with k and are returned as strings. A different conditional draw law would require a different state/recurrence, not silently the same iid calculation.

title: Worst-model log growth, including a kink optimum
prompt: net_returns is a list of n integer NET returns in [−100,100], 1≤n≤50. weights is a matrix of m model rows, 1≤m≤30; each row has n integer counts in [0,10^9] with positive sum. Row j assigns state probabilities count/row_sum. This is a SET of models with no assigned model probabilities. Exposure f changes positive wealth by multiplier 1+f×net_return. cap is a finite float in [0,1]. For every state with nonzero weight in ANY model, 1+cap×net_return≥10^−4 is guaranteed, ensuring positive wealth throughout [0,cap]. States zero in every model are irrelevant; do not evaluate their invalid logarithms. Maximise WORST-MODEL expected natural-log growth over 0≤f≤cap. Return [fraction,growth], two finite floats accurate to absolute 10^−7; growth is the MINIMUM model log expectation at the chosen fraction. Choose the smallest maximising fraction: if a model gives no positive expected return, zero is optimal and this tie rule selects it, including an identically zero model. No fees, extra outcomes, drawdown constraints or simulation. Preserve all inputs. The worst-model curve is concave but can be NONDIFFERENTIABLE where its active model changes. Do not average model probabilities, optimise model roots independently or apply the binary 2p−1 formula to general returns. Use a bounded one-dimensional concave search; O(120mn) numerical work and O(mn) stored model probabilities is sufficient under these bounds. Use log1p for small f×return and accurate summation; do not round the output.
explanation:
For each model j, define \(g_j(f)=\sum_i p_{ji}\log(1+fr_i)\), where \(r_i\) is its net return and \(p_{ji}\) its normalised state probability. The positivity condition covers the UNION of reachable states, while zero-weight terms need no logarithm. Each g_j is concave; its pointwise minimum h is concave because every g_j at an interior convex combination is at least the same combination of endpoint h values. With a positive-mean nonconstant model, g_j is strictly concave. If ANY model has nonpositive mean return, concavity and its derivative at zero imply g_j(f)≤g_j(0)=0 for nonnegative f. Since h(0)=0, choose zero; an all-zero model is handled without an arbitrary positive stake. Otherwise every model has positive mean and strict curvature; for cap>0, h initially increases and has a unique maximum, which may occur at a boundary or a kink. Ternary search uses concavity without differentiating the minimum; compare cap and zero explicitly after narrowing. There is no need to infer which model is active near a numerical crossing.

In sample three, the two curves cross at a nonzero root of \((1-f)^8=(1+f)^7(1-9f)\). One is increasing and the other decreasing there, so the MINIMUM peaks at that kink, about 0.07547246, not at either separate model optimum or an averaged distribution’s optimum. This bounded scalar model-set calculation does not address estimation, drawdown or action-dependent learning. Probabilities are normalised once, log1p retains small increments, and fsum reduces summation loss; finite binary64 accuracy is checked against independent high-precision objectives and closed-form/polynomial roots.

title: Aggregate shared loadings before squaring risk
prompt: Centred unit cash payoffs satisfy \(Y_i=\sum_j b_{ij}F_j+\varepsilon_i\), where \(b_{ij}\) is loadings[i][j]. quantities gives n fixed signed INTEGER position quantities, 1≤n≤1000; loadings is an n by k integer matrix, 0≤k≤20. Each factor F_j has integer variance factor_variances[j]; residual ε_i has integer variance residual_variances[i]. All factors and residuals are pairwise uncorrelated with finite second moments. Quantities and loadings are in [−10^6,10^6]; variances in [0,10^6]. All dimensions match. Return {"exposures":[signed_integer_strings],"factor_variance":integer_string,"residual_variance":integer_string,"variance":integer_string} for the combined CASH payoff \(\sum_i q_iY_i\), where \(q_i\) is quantities[i]. Every number must be a canonical decimal STRING; zero is "0". Means, fees, funding and higher moments are outside this task. Preserve all inputs. Use O(n(k+1)) integer arithmetic/\(O(k)\) auxiliary integers, with bit costs additional. Do not normalise quantities into portfolio weights or square each position loading before aggregating a shared factor.
explanation: The combined loading on factor j is the SIGNED sum \(a_j=\sum_i q_i b_{ij}\). Pairwise uncorrelated factors and residuals give factor variance \(\sum_j a_j^2\operatorname{Var}(F_j)\) and residual variance \(\sum_i q_i^2\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)\). A shared factor must be summed before it is squared; opposing exposures can cancel that factor while residual terms remain. Independence is stronger than necessary for this second-moment calculation. Empty factor lists leave only residual risk; zero factor variances do not make nonzero reported exposures disappear. A single pass accumulates the k exposures and residual scalar; exact Python integers and decimal strings preserve large squared quantities in the browser. This computes risk under the supplied model, not an empirical covariance estimate or an execution guarantee.

title: Average the worst probability mass of the whole book
prompt: scenario_pnl is an m by n integer matrix of JOINT unit cash payoffs for fixed same-horizon scenarios, 1≤m≤5000 and 1≤n≤20. quantities has n signed integer quantities. weights has m integer probability COUNTS in [0,10^6] with positive total W. Pnl entries and quantities are in [−10^6,10^6]. Each portfolio cash LOSS is \(L_s=-\sum_i q_iP_{si}\), where \(q_i\) is quantities[i] and \(P_{si}\) is scenario_pnl[s][i]. Supplied payoffs already include all stated costs/exits: do not subtract them again. tail=[a,b], integers 1≤a≤b≤10^6, specifies alpha=a/b. Sort positive-mass scenarios by DESCENDING loss and take exactly the worst alpha fraction of total probability, splitting the final scenario mass if necessary. Return {"threshold":signed_integer_string,"tail_mean":[signed_numerator_string,positive_denominator_string]}. threshold is the SMALLEST loss used with positive mass in that selected tail, including when the cutoff is an exact boundary. tail_mean is the exact average loss in the selected probability mass. Losses may be NEGATIVE; never clamp profits to zero. Equal losses, duplicate scenarios and zero counts are permitted. Rationals must be reduced canonical decimal strings, with zero=["0","1"]. Preserve all inputs. Use O(mn+m log m) arithmetic/comparisons and O(m) auxiliary records, with integer bit/gcd costs additional. Aggregate the JOINT book before sorting; averaging whole scenario records or summing independently selected component tails is wrong. This is a specified finite-distribution tail measure, not an estimated probability or a guaranteed funding limit.
explanation: First aggregate each joint scenario into the actual signed book loss. Weight counts describe probability mass, not equally likely scenario rows. Multiply count masses by b, so total scaled mass is Wb and the requested tail is the INTEGER amount Wa. Descending losses receive up to w_s b units until exactly Wa units are allocated. Their weighted loss numerator divided by Wa is the tail mean; the final positive allocation identifies the explicitly defined threshold. Splitting an atom is essential: sample one uses one count at loss ten and one-and-a-half counts at loss four, producing (10+1.5·4)/2.5=\(\frac{32}{5}\). Taking every observation at or above the cutoff would instead average a different probability mass. Duplicate equal losses do not change the answer, and zero-count states are excluded before threshold selection. Alpha one recovers the full expected loss, which may be negative. Sample two has opposite unit movements but an identically zero book; summing two separate component tails would invent book losses. Exact integer scaling avoids rounding the tail size or a large rational numerator.

title: Choose trades under shared-factor and gross-capital limits
prompt: There are n indivisible opportunities, 0≤n≤40. Integer lists gains, loadings and margins have length n: gain_i in [−10^6,10^6] is the declared expected NET cash payoff if selected once; loading_i in [−10,10] is its signed exposure to one centred variance-one common factor; margin_i in [1,80] is required gross capital. Write \(g_i\)=gains[i], \(\ell_i\)=loadings[i] and \(m_i\)=margins[i]. The stylised payoff is \(g_i+\ell_iF\), with no residual risks. A chosen subset I has expected payoff \(\sum_{i\in I}g_i\), factor loading \(\sum_{i\in I}\ell_i\) and variance \((\sum_{i\in I}\ell_i)^2\). Choose once BEFORE outcomes. Integer capital in [0,80] bounds \(\sum_{i\in I}m_i\); integer exposure_limit in [0,400] requires \(\left|\sum_{i\in I}\ell_i\right|\leq\texttt{exposure\_limit}\) at the FINAL book. Margins do not net, even for opposing exposures. Empty selection is allowed. Maximise total expected gain; ties prefer lower total margin, then fewer selected opportunities, then lexicographically smaller SORTED original index list. Return {"gain":integer,"margin":integer,"indices":[indices]}. Preserve all inputs. Negative-gain opportunities must not be discarded automatically: they can make a desirable combined exposure feasible. Do not prune an intermediate loading merely because it exceeds the FINAL limit; later positions may offset it. With B=capital and A=sum(abs(loadings)), use a dynamic program that selects each opportunity at most once, with O(n(B+1)(2A+1)) score transitions and O((B+1)(2A+1)) stored score/reconstruction states. State counts are finite; exact bit masks may use \(O(n)\) bits per state for reconstruction. This is a discrete specified selection model, not a live profitability or funding certification. No borrowing, partial trades, changing gains after outcomes or assumed zero covariance among these common-factor payoffs.
explanation:
A state records exact used gross capital and SIGNED factor loading after an item prefix. Keep the best expected gain for that state; on equal gains keep fewer trades, then the lexicographically smaller original-index list. All future choices affect two equal-state prefixes identically, so this dominance preserves the final objective and tie rules. Read transitions from the previous prefix and write into a copied next map: each opportunity is selected at most once. A load of +10 followed by −10 is feasible at final limit zero, so applying the final risk test during intermediate layers would discard sample one; so would discarding the negative-gain hedge. Gross margins add even when factor exposure cancels.

For compact exact reconstruction, give earlier indices more significant bits. When selection counts tie, the larger mask has the smaller first differing index and therefore the lexicographically smaller sorted list. Prefix dominance stores (gain,negative_count,mask). The final comparison additionally prefers smaller capital BEFORE fewer items. Empty selection supplies zero gain and zero capital. The possible capital coordinates are 0..B and exposure coordinates −A..A, where A is the sum of absolute input loadings; each item considers at most their product, rather than enumerating all 2^n subsets. Masks carry up to n bits and are internal, never an approximate numeric risk measure. This exact constrained optimum inherits every assumption and omitted risk of the supplied single-factor model.

title: Aggregate signed Greeks with their contract multipliers
prompt: positions contains up to 10000 rows [quantity,multiplier,delta_num,gamma_num,theta_num]. Quantity is an integer in [−10^6,10^6]; multiplier is a positive integer ≤10^6. All sensitivity numerators are integers in [−10^6,10^6] and share positive integer sensitivity_denominator D≤10^9. These are per-unit delta, gamma and CALENDAR-TIME theta, with theta per DAY. stock_units is an integer in [−10^6,10^6]; stock contributes delta stock_units and zero gamma/theta. move is an integer underlying price change in [−10^6,10^6], and days is an integer in [0,10^6]. Other inputs, financing and fees are held fixed. Aggregate SIGNED quantities/multipliers first. Write \(x=\texttt{move}\), \(h=\texttt{days}\), and compute the retained Taylor change \(\Delta x+\tfrac12\Gamma x^2+\Theta h\). Return {"delta":[num_text,den_text],"gamma":[num_text,den_text],"theta":[num_text,den_text],"change":[num_text,den_text]}, all exact reduced canonical decimal STRINGS with positive denominators; zero=["0","1"]. Preserve positions. Use \(O(n)\) integer arithmetic/O(1) working integers, with bit/gcd costs additional. The retained quantity is computed exactly as algebra; it is a local value approximation for a general instrument, especially unreliable for arbitrary large moves. Do not omit the half factor, change theta to a remaining-time derivative, or treat the output as terminal payoff or guaranteed trading profit.
explanation: Use D as the common denominator for each aggregate sensitivity. Stock delta starts at stock_units·D; each row adds quantity·multiplier times each numerator. A short position reverses ALL of that contract’s contributions. Write d,g,t for the aggregate sensitivity numerators, x for move and h for days. The retained change has common denominator 2D and numerator \(2dx+gx^2+2th\). Reduce each result separately. This keeps the half-gamma coefficient, signed theta and stated day units without floating arithmetic. For sample one, the stock neutralises delta but aggregate gamma four/time contribution minus six remain, giving forty-four. Local initial delta cancellation does not maintain neutrality after a move; summing these numbers is not a self-financing rehedging calculation. Large exact strings survive display and copied cases.

title: Evaluate a signed option book at every terminal price
prompt: contracts contains up to 20000 rows [kind,strike,quantity,multiplier]. kind is "call" or "put"; strike is an integer in [0,10^9], quantity in [−10^6,10^6], and multiplier in [1,10^6]. All European contracts use the SAME nonnegative terminal underlying price and maturity. Each unit call pays max(S−strike,0), each put max(strike−S,0). stock_units is an integer in [−10^6,10^6]; cash is a fixed TERMINAL cash payment in [−10^9,10^9], possibly a liability. prices contains up to 20000 integer terminal prices in [0,10^9], in arbitrary order with duplicates. Return the exact combined TERMINAL cash payoff at each price, including stock_units·S+cash, as canonical signed decimal STRINGS in original query order; zero is "0". Do not subtract premiums or reinterpret terminal cash as its present value. Preserve every input. Use sorting and slope changes or equivalent preprocessing, avoiding a scan through every contract for every query: O(n log n+m log m) arithmetic/comparisons and O(n+m) storage is sufficient. Integer bit costs are additional. Handle shared strikes, calls/puts at zero strike, negative quantities, exact strike prices and empty lists. A signed book need not be convex; slope jumps can be negative. No volatility model, early exercise, simulation or Greek approximation is involved.
solution:
def solve(contracts, stock_units, cash, prices):
    events = {}
    slope = stock_units
    value = cash
    for kind,strike,quantity,multiplier in contracts:
        amount = quantity*multiplier
        events[strike] = events.get(strike,0)+amount
        if kind == 'put':
            slope -= amount
            value += amount*strike
    cuts = sorted(events)
    cursor = 0
    previous = 0
    answer = [None]*len(prices)
    for index in sorted(range(len(prices)),key=lambda i:prices[i]):
        price = prices[index]
        while cursor < len(cuts) and cuts[cursor] <= price:
            strike = cuts[cursor]
            value += slope*(strike-previous)
            slope += events[strike]
            previous = strike
            cursor += 1
        answer[index] = str(value+slope*(price-previous))
    return answer
explanation: At price zero the book value is terminal cash plus every signed put amount times strike; its initial right-hand slope starts at stock units minus all put amounts. At each strike, BOTH a call and a put add their signed amount to the slope: a call begins paying above its strike, while a put stops losing one unit of payoff per added stock-price unit. Combine events sharing a strike. Advance the value continuously to each event, change the slope there, then evaluate sorted queries in the current linear segment. At a strike either adjoining segment gives the same payoff; processing the event before the equal-price query is safe. Restore the original query order. Zero-strike put events cancel their provisional initial slope; signed events can cancel or create negative curvature. The stock/cash piece is already a terminal linear payment. This exact piecewise calculation does not price the options, include premiums or use local sensitivities.

title: Validate call quotes and bound an unquoted strike exactly
prompt: Use a ONE-period, zero-interest, no-dividend pricing class defined by \(C(K)=E[(S_T-K)^+]\) and \(E[S_T]=S_0\), with a NONNEGATIVE probability measure supported on [0,M]. Zero masses are explicitly allowed; no physical probabilities or strictly-positive-support condition are imposed. M=max_price is an integer in [1,10^9]. price_denominator D is an integer in [1,10^9]; spot_numerator and call_numerators are integers in [0,10^9]. Spot is S₀=spot_numerator/D. strikes is a strictly increasing list of n integers with 0<K<M, n≤20000; call_numerators has matching length and quote i is call_numerators[i]/D. queries contains m≤20000 integer strikes in [0,M], arbitrarily ordered with duplicates. Input dimensions/order are guaranteed, but quote FEASIBILITY is not. Return {"feasible":False,"bounds":None} if NO such probability measure matches all quotes/spot. Otherwise return {"feasible":True,"bounds":[[lower_pair,upper_pair],...]} in query order, with SHARP inclusive price bounds over ALL matching measures. Each pair is [signed_numerator_text,positive_denominator_text], exact reduced canonical decimal STRINGS; zero=["0","1"]. A quoted strike and endpoints have fixed prices. Preserve all lists. Aim for O(n+m log(n+2)) exact arithmetic/comparisons and O(n+m) auxiliary storage; bit/gcd costs are additional. Use collective convexity, decreasing slopes and endpoint slope bounds, not independent pairwise price tests or a linear-programming package. The support cap matters. These inclusive bounds describe the declared NONNEGATIVE-measure class; they do not prove strict no-arbitrage for a different specified physical support in which every state must have positive probability.
explanation:
Add the known endpoint quotes C(0)=S₀ and C(M)=0. A bounded nonnegative expectation gives a continuous convex decreasing call curve, with strike slope between −1 and zero. In scaled numerators, adjacent secant slopes must therefore be nondecreasing, between −D and zero. Check every secant by integer cross multiplication, including the first/last bounds and S₀≤M. These are also SUFFICIENT: linearly join the quotes, extend slope −1 left of zero and zero right of M, and put probability mass equal to each nonnegative slope jump divided by D at its knot. The jumps sum to one; the resulting call expectations equal the curve and its mean is C(0).

For a query K strictly between adjacent knots a,b with prices A,B, the largest feasible price is their chord. A new price cannot fall below the line through A with the PREVIOUS secant slope, or the line through B with the NEXT secant slope. Use synthetic boundary slopes −1 and zero where those neighbouring intervals do not exist. Thus

\[\begin{aligned}L&=\max\{A+s_L(K-a),\\&\qquad B-s_R(b-K)\},\end{aligned}\]

\[\begin{aligned}U&=\frac{A(b-K)}{b-a}\\&\quad+\frac{B(K-a)}{b-a}.\end{aligned}\]

Any inserted price in [L,U] maintains all adjacent slope inequalities; the SAME slope-jump construction yields a matching measure on the augmented knots. This proves sharpness over continuous terminal support, not merely a fixed grid or numerical sample. Equality/zero mass is allowed by this task’s class. Each query is bounded separately: its extremising measure need not attain every OTHER query bound simultaneously. Binary-search the interval, calculate the two lower candidate rationals and the chord with integer products, compare exactly, and reduce each pair. For the first example at strike one hundred, both supporting lines give twenty while the chord gives thirty-five. Merely interpolating the old quotes would select one admissible price, not establish a unique implied price. No probability forecast, Black–Scholes parameter or extra empirical regularity was supplied.

title: Decompose a weighted Brier score without rounding
prompt:
probabilities, outcomes and weights are equal-length lists, with 1≤n≤50000. Forecast ticks p are integers in [0,D], where scale D is an integer in [1,10^9]; the actual forecast is p/D. Outcomes are zero or one. Weights are integers in [0,10^9], with positive total W; they represent evaluation mass, not necessarily independent repetitions. There are at most FIFTY distinct forecast ticks. Group records by EXACTLY IDENTICAL forecast ticks, discarding zero-weight groups. For group \(g\), define weighted mass \(N_g\), weighted success mass \(S_g\), forecast \(f_g=p_g/D\) and rate \(r_g=S_g/N_g\); define global rate \(r=\sum_i w_i y_i/W\). Return a dict with these four exact quantities:

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm{score}&=\sum_i w_i(f_i-y_i)^2/W,\\\mathrm{reliability}&=\sum_g N_g(f_g-r_g)^2/W,\\\mathrm{resolution}&=\sum_g N_g(r_g-r)^2/W,\\\mathrm{uncertainty}&=r(1-r).\end{aligned}\]

Each value must be ONE reduced fraction STRING "numerator/denominator", with canonical decimal integers and a positive denominator; zero is "\(\texttt{0/1}\)". Preserve all inputs. Use O(n+g) arithmetic operations and O(g) group state, g≤50; integer bit/gcd costs are additional. Do not use floats, merge nearby forecasts into coarse bins, or treat small empirical reliability as proof of population calibration. The identity score=uncertainty−resolution+reliability must hold for this exact grouping.
explanation: The grouping is part of the mathematics. Let \(A=\sum_iw_i p_i^2\), \(B=\sum_iw_i p_i y_i\), \(S=\sum_iw_i y_i\) and \(W=\sum_iw_i\). Aggregate each exact forecast level into (N_g,S_g), then form the rational \(T=\sum_g S_g^2/N_g\). Direct loss is (A−2DB+D²S)/(WD²). Expanding the group squares gives reliability (A−2DB)/(WD²)+T/W; resolution is T/W−S²/W²; uncertainty is S/W−S²/W². Their signed combination cancels T and S²/W² to recover direct score. Within a group, y²=y and the forecast is constant; a coarse bin with different forecasts would lose terms, just as in the paired-record interview problem. Reduce the sum T after every addition using gcd, and reduce each returned fraction. Zero weights carry no evaluation mass. In sample one the two exact rates equal their forecasts, giving reliability zero and resolution \(\frac{1}{16}\). This is a finite weighted identity; empirical rates and resolution can overfit without validating future forecasts.

title: Choose a bid using the value–rival joint law
prompt: states contains 1≤n≤20000 rows [net_value, highest_rival_bid, weight]. These describe a discrete JOINT law already conditional on your observed information: value V is an integer in [−10^9,10^9], highest rival bid H is an integer in [0,10^9], and weight is an integer in [0,10^9], with positive total W. Negative V represents a net terminal value after liabilities. cap is an integer in [0,10^9]. Choose an INTEGER bid b∈[0,cap]. You win only when b>H; ties LOSE. On a win, gain is V−b; otherwise zero. Rival laws stay fixed when choosing b; no independence or equilibrium is assumed. Maximise expected gain, breaking ties by the SMALLEST bid. Return {"bid":b,"gain":fraction_text,"win_probability":fraction_text,"win_value":fraction_text_or_None}. The latter is E[V|winning at the SELECTED bid], or None for zero winning mass. Every fraction is a reduced canonical decimal STRING "numerator/positive_denominator"; zero is "\(\texttt{0/1}\)". Preserve the input. Use O(n log n) comparisons/arithmetic and \(O(n)\) auxiliary storage or better, with integer bit/gcd costs additional; do not scan every bid through cap. Evaluate duplicate rival thresholds as one complete group. A fixed conditional winning value cannot be used unchanged to optimise all actions.
explanation: Start with bid zero, which wins no states because H is nonnegative and ties lose. Its gain is zero. The winning set changes only at b=H+1. Between two consecutive such INTEGER breakpoints, winning mass and weighted value stay fixed, while subtracting b times positive winning mass makes gain decrease. Therefore only zero and distinct thresholds H+1≤cap can be optimal; extra zero-mass thresholds do not invalidate this reasoning. Sort by H and add EVERY row sharing a threshold before evaluating its candidate. Maintain cumulative mass M and weighted value A. Candidate gain numerator is A−bM over the common denominator W, so compare integers without rounding. Process bids ascending and update only on strictly greater gain to retain the smallest bid on ties. Remember the chosen M and A for win probability M/W and value A/M; use None when M=0. The conditional mean can be much higher than the selected bid and changes at each new winning set. In sample one, admitting all four states at bid twenty-one beats the narrow low-threshold subset; cap twenty instead makes that admission impossible. Summaries that keep only marginal means of V and H cannot replace their joint pairing. This is risk-neutral optimisation under a declared fixed law, not an inferred auction equilibrium.
